title: UK doctor infected with Ebola being treated at London hospital
content:
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been flown back to the UK.
The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.
It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.
Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low.
The infected doctor was brought to the UK on a medical evacuation flight as part of a joint effort by the UK and DR Congo governments and their international health partners, the Department of Health (DoH) said.
A convoy of emergency vehicles were on hand to complete the transfer following the man's arrival at the RAF base.
Three large police vans travelled at either end of the convey, while two ambulances and another support car were involved.
Traffic was stopped and police exited the vans to keep the public away as the convey arrived at the Royal Free Hospital.
The man is now being treated in a "highly specialised"  isolation unit at the hospital, the DoH said.
The Royal Free Hospital successfully treated three health workers who had been evacuated after the Ebola outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and 2015.
There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.
None of these cases have resulted in a death.
There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa in the 2010s.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.
Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fuelled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.
There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organization said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.
The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.
It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.

title: Kenyan pharmacists warn against viral craze of using allergy drug for vaginal tightening
content:
Kenyan pharmacists have warned women against inserting allergy tablets into their vaginas in an attempt to make them tighter, following the spread of potentially dangerous medical advice on social media.
The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure.
Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles.
"Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said.
"Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. Cetirizine tablets are made to be swallowed. Their ingredients have not been tested on delicate vaginal tissue," it added.
Cetirizine is commonly used to relieve symptoms such as sneezing, a runny nose, itchy eyes and skin reactions, including hives.
The controversy began earlier this week when posts circulated on TikTok claiming that cetirizine could reduce vaginal moisture and create a sensation of tightness during sex.
This sparked widespread debate, with some users promoting the practice while others questioned its safety.
There have also been local media reports of the price of the drug rising and increased demand in some pharmacies, especially in the capital, Nairobi.
"Cetirizine is an allergy medicine, taken by mouth. It is not approved or tested for any other purpose, and definitely not for vaginal use," the PSK, a professional body representing pharmacists in Kenya, said in a statement issued on Thursday.
"If you have already tried it. Stop. See a doctor if you have pain, bleeding, burning, itching, unusual discharge, or fever," it advised.
The society also urged social media influencers and content creators to take care when sharing health information, saying that unverified claims could put people's health at risk.
The warning comes a day after Kenya's health ministry expressed concern about the trend.
Ouma Oluga, a senior health official, said some social media users appeared to be treating the medical advice from experts as a joke, without considering the possible consequences.
He suggested that the authorities could introduce a system to track the distribution and purchase of medicines to help identify possible misuse.
However, no formal decision has been announced on such a initiative.
The PSK said it was aware of reports of increased demand for cetirizine, rising prices and shortages at some pharmacies.
It urged retailers not to exploit the trend, warning that people who genuinely needed the medicine for allergies could struggle to obtain it.
It went on to encourage its members not to knowingly dispense medicines that would be misused - and report any side affects to the health authorities of those that had been.
The PSK ended its statement by saying that unverified online trends should never trump what the experts say: "Check with a pharmacist before using any medicine for a purpose it was not made for.

title: Wisconsin infant is US’ third measles-related death this week
content: An infant in Wisconsin has died in connection with an large, ongoing measles outbreak, the state health department said Thursday. The death marks the first measles-related death in Wisconsin in more than 35 years and the third reported in the US this week. “My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state’s health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” The health department said the coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles. To protect the family’s privacy, the department will not release any additional details about the child, officials said. Wisconsin is experiencing its largest measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of Thursday, Wisconsin has recorded 431 cases in 13 counties this years. The state’s health department cautions that the true number is most certainly higher because not everyone who gets sick seeks medical care. To compare, Wisconsin had 36 cases in 2025. In the past, most cases were associated with international travel. Now, cases are now spreading through domestic travel, as well as through exposure to family members and others in the community. Nine people in Wisconsin have been hospitalized. While anyone with measles can develop life-threatening complications such as pneumonia or swelling of the brain, children younger than 5, people with weak immune systems and people who are pregnant face a higher risk of severe disease. The state is encouraging everyone who hasn’t been vaccinated to receive a measles vaccine. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. Health officials said the rate of MMR vaccination among kindergarteners in Wisconsin is at about 85%, well below the roughly 95% coverage needed to prevent measles from spreading through a population. “That’s really the central issue here: Measles is now spreading because there are enough people who are susceptible to infection for the virus to continue finding new hosts,” said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, Wisconsin’s chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases. Wisconsin’s health department updated its guidance this week to recommend an early dose of MMR vaccine for certain infants between 6 and 11 months of age who are at increased risk of exposure during the outbreak. Typically, MMR vaccination doesn’t start until a child’s first birthday. Until 2025, there had been no measles deaths in the US for years. Three measles-related deaths have already been reported this week. In Pennsylvania, an unvaccinated resident of rural Jefferson County, in the north-central part of the state, died after testing positive for measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Wednesday. It was the sixth person in Pennsylvania to die from measles this year. On Monday, the New York State Department of Health announced that a child had died after contracting measles. The child lived in rural Lewis County, in the northern part of the state. The child’s death marked New York’s first in 30 years . More than 4,800 measles cases have been reported across the US this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the most since 1991, almost a decade before measles was declared eliminated in the US. An international meeting to determine the status of measles elimination in the United States is scheduled to take place next week.

A soft implant that attaches without stitches lowered blood pressure in rats, pointing toward a way to treat hypertension with less damage to surrounding tissue. Nearly half of all adults in the United States have high blood pressure, a leading cause of heart disease. Medications and changes to diet or lifestyle can help, but roughly one in 10 people with the condition has drug-resistant hypertension. For these patients, controlling blood pressure can become a persistent challenge. “For many patients, even taking a combination of three to five medicines doesn’t alleviate their high blood pressure,” said Tao Zhou, the study’s corresponding author and the Wormley Family Early Career Assistant Professor of Engineering Science and Mechanics at Penn State . “In these cases, bioelectronic devices that use electrical signals to modulate the body’s natural response systems offer a promising form of alternative treatment.” Zhou is also affiliated with Penn State’s Center for Neural Engineering, Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences, and Materials Research Institute. Zhou and his colleagues have developed CaroFlex, a soft, stretchy, 3D-printed device that attaches to an artery and delivers gentle electrical stimulation. In a rodent model, it lowered blood pressure while causing much less damage to surrounding tissue, the researchers reported in a paper recently published in Device . The device works through a pressure-control system the body already has. Specialized nerve endings called baroreceptors detect changes in how much artery walls stretch. They trigger the baroreceptor reflex, or baroreflex, which helps regulate blood pressure, including by changing how tightly blood vessels constrict. Baroreceptors occur throughout the body, with many concentrated in the carotid sinus, a small region near where the carotid artery branches. This artery carries oxygen-rich blood to the head and neck. Applying electrical stimulation at the carotid sinus can activate those receptors and engage the reflex to lower blood pressure, Zhou explained. To test whether CaroFlex could do this in a living animal, the researchers implanted it at the carotid sinus in rats. Sensors on the animals’ bodies monitored blood pressure during a 10-minute testing window. Four of the five electrical frequencies tested reduced blood pressure, with readings falling by more than 15% on average. When the researchers examined tissues in contact with CaroFlex after two weeks, they found no apparent damage or immune response. A few commercially available devices already use electrical stimulation to engage this reflex. The engineering challenge is keeping an electrode connected to an artery that continually stretches and shrinks. Conventional devices are generally made from rigid metals and plastics, which do not fit the mechanical behavior of soft tissue well. “These devices are usually held in place with stitches,” Zhou said. “These stitches can cause damage to the devices, and more importantly, the tissues they’re integrated with over time, as arteries stretch and shrink to help move blood around the body.” CaroFlex is made primarily from hydrogel, a soft, jelly-like material that better matches the tissue’s flexibility. Conductive hydrogels form the electrodes that deliver electrical stimulation, while adhesive hydrogels provide a strong, nontoxic attachment designed to let the device stick painlessly to biological tissue without stitches. The team used 3D printing to build this combination of electrical and adhesive components. Laboratory tests on tissue samples examined whether the materials could provide both flexibility and a dependable attachment. CaroFlex stretched to more than twice its original size before breaking. Its adhesive film maintained strong, continuous adhesion, including when made from mixtures that had been stored for six months. The researchers also compared CaroFlex with traditional platinum bioelectrodes. By passing electrical currents through each type, they measured how the different materials affected conductivity. CaroFlex adhered more closely to the tissue and provided a more reliable electrical connection than the conventional electrodes, the team reported. With CaroFlex shown to function in living tissue and evidence of tissue compatibility, Zhou said the next steps are to fine-tune its effectiveness and scale up the approach. The eventual goal is clinical trials to test it as a treatment for hypertension in humans. “Our lab is actively leading several developments in 3D-printed bioelectronics for use across the body, which is exciting,” Zhou said. “This fabrication approach allows us to design, fabricate, and adapt bioelectronics for potential clinical trials and commercial distribution much more efficiently than traditional methods of manufacturing.” Reference: “3D printable suture-free bioadhesive electronic interface for hypertension therapy” by Marzia Momin, Salahuddin Ahmed, Arafat Hossain, Jia Sun, Xinyi Wang, Basma AlMahmood, Jiashu Ren, Li-Pang Huang, Umar Farooq, John Bisognano and Tao Zhou, 5 May 2026, Device . DOI: 10.1016/j.device.2026.101150 This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental health implications. Could the amount of sugar we consume before birth and during infancy influence our mental health decades later? An experiment rooted in postwar Britain suggests that the effects of our earliest diets may extend far beyond childhood. During World War II and the years that followed, the United Kingdom strictly rationed sugar, limiting how much families could purchase. When those restrictions ended in September 1953, sugar consumption surged, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to examine how early-life exposure to sugar might shape long-term health. A study published in General Psychiatry found that exposure to rationing during early life was associated with a 17% lower risk of anxiety and a 14% lower risk of depression compared with no exposure. The researchers analyzed data from 66,223 UK Biobank participants born around the policy change, linking the timing of their earliest years to health records later in life. Because the availability of other foods remained relatively stable when sugar consumption increased, the end of rationing offered a natural experiment. Researchers could compare people who experienced different periods of restricted sugar availability at the start of life. They estimated exposure using birth dates relative to the policy change, with exposure ranging from before birth only to periods extending through about age two. That approach tracked exposure to a national policy, rather than measuring what individual mothers or children ate. The researchers did not have individual childhood food records, and unmeasured factors, including other aspects of maternal diet, may have influenced the results. The findings therefore cannot establish that lower sugar intake caused the differences in mental health. The strongest associations appeared among people exposed to rationing throughout the first 1,000 days after conception, spanning pregnancy and roughly the first two years after birth. Compared with people without early exposure, this group had approximately 24% lower relative risk of anxiety and 21% lower relative risk of depression. Across the analysis, the association generally strengthened with longer exposure to rationing. For participants exposed throughout those first 1,000 days, diagnoses also appeared later in their health records. The first recorded anxiety diagnosis occurred about two years later, and the first recorded depression diagnosis about four years later, than among participants with no early exposure. These findings concern when diagnoses were first recorded, rather than necessarily when symptoms began. Early nutrition could potentially influence later mental health through its effects on stress regulation, inflammation, and brain development. The authors drew these possible explanations from previous research, but did not directly test the mechanisms in the UK Biobank analysis. Further studies that measure individual diets and examine other populations will help clarify how dietary conditions during pregnancy and infancy relate to mental health across the life course, and what that relationship could mean for public health. Reference: “Sugar restriction during the first 1000 days after conception and its association with decreased risk of anxiety and depression” by Xiuping Dou, Yang Su, Yao Huang, Man He, Bingying Zhang, Xuejin Li, Hualiang Lin and Yin Yang, 7 July 2026, General Psychiatry . DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70038 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

An observational study of middle-aged men links animal protein to lower testosterone and plant protein to higher levels, but the differences are small, and their health effects remain unclear. A protein-rich meal gives the body amino acids, the building blocks it needs to make and repair tissues, including muscle. Testosterone helps regulate muscle growth and also supports bones and sexual function. Food provides essential materials, while hormones help direct what the body does with them. That connection makes diet a reasonable place to look when studying testosterone, yet relatively few studies have examined its relationship with protein intake. Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that men who consumed more animal protein tended to have lower total testosterone levels in their blood. Those who consumed more plant protein tended to have higher levels. The findings do not mean that higher testosterone is necessarily healthier or that one protein source improves hormone function. The research, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , included 2,546 men aged 42 to 60 living in eastern Finland. It drew on the university’s ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study. Researchers assessed the men’s diets using four-day food records collected between 1984 and 1989 and measured total testosterone in blood samples. They also measured sex hormone-binding globulin, or SHBG, a protein that binds to sex hormones and influences total testosterone concentrations in the blood. Looking at individual foods revealed a distinction that the broad category of animal protein could obscure. Higher dairy protein intake was associated with lower total testosterone and SHBG levels. Meat protein intake was associated with lower SHBG, but it had no association with total testosterone. Among plant foods, higher protein intake from vegetables and sources other than cereal products was associated with higher total testosterone. To compare the differences, the researchers divided the men into four groups according to their protein intake. Those in the highest animal protein group had total testosterone concentrations averaging 1.2 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L) below those in the lowest group. For plant protein, the highest intake group averaged 1.1 nmol/L above the lowest group. SHBG showed similar opposing associations with animal and plant protein intake. “Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health,” says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland. Age, excess weight, and lifestyle can influence testosterone levels. The analyses accounted for the men’s age and body mass index, along with several other dietary, lifestyle, and health factors. Even with those adjustments, other aspects of their diets or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that eating particular proteins caused the hormone differences. It also cannot determine whether consuming different protein sources affects how much testosterone the body produces or how the hormone acts in the body. Reference: “Associations of dietary proteins with serum total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations in middle-aged men” by Miika M. Wynne-Ellis, Heli E. K. Virtanen, Elizabeth Bertone-Johnson, Sari Hantunen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, Jukka T. Salonen and Jyrki K. Virtanen, 9 September 2026, International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition . DOI: 10.1080/09637486.2026.2731397 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

A beginner’s violin lesson may seem worlds apart from dementia research, yet wearable brain scans are revealing signals that could help scientists understand both learning and neurological disease. Playing a familiar tune on a violin is no simple task for someone who has never held the instrument. Each movement must produce the intended sound, and the brain has to learn how to coordinate those movements. Researchers at the University of Nottingham have now captured changes in brain activity as beginners learned to play, revealing measurable differences after just one violin lesson. The study, published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience , involved 22 novice violin players. Using a wearable brain scanner, the scientists tracked patterns of neural activity while participants attempted to play “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They found that those who improved the most also showed the greatest changes in certain brain signals associated with movement and learning. Capturing those signals while someone plays an instrument presents a technical challenge. The electrical activity of neurons generates extremely weak magnetic fields, which can be measured to study brain function. However, the equipment must be sensitive enough to detect these signals without interference, while still allowing the person being studied to move naturally. The researchers used a technology called OPM-MEG, developed in Nottingham, that incorporates brain-scanning sensors into a lightweight helmet connected to a backpack-mounted control unit. Unlike scanning systems that restrict movement, this wearable design allows researchers to monitor brain activity as people perform everyday tasks. There was still one problem. A conventional violin contains metal components that would interfere with the scanner’s measurements. To overcome this obstacle, the team enlisted Alan Kirby, an expert violinist and violin maker from Nottingham. Kirby sourced a standard violin and replaced every metal part with alternatives he crafted himself, producing an entirely wooden instrument operating at frequencies associated with Baroque music. “Bringing together the ancient art of violin making, with the quantum physics underpinning this brain scanner, has been amazing. Perhaps even more impressive was to actually see the effects of my lessons on peoples brains. That was quite an experience,” Kirby said. Kirby also served as the participants’ violin instructor. At the beginning of the experiment, all 22 beginners watched a video of him playing “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They then attempted to perform the same melody during their first scanning session, while the researchers recorded their brain activity. After completing that initial recording, the participants received a violin lesson from Kirby. They then returned for a second scanning session, following the same procedure and attempting to play the tune again. By comparing recordings from before and after the lesson, the researchers could examine how the brain responded to a brief period of musical training. Their attention focused on brain waves, rhythmic fluctuations in electrical activity that occur across groups of neurons. In particular, they examined oscillations in the beta frequency range, which are thought to help signal whether an action produces the result the brain expects. When learning the violin, that process could involve predicting the sound of a note before playing it and registering whether the actual sound matches the prediction. Unexpected notes provide information that the movement did not produce the intended outcome. “Your brain works by making predictions about what will happen as a result of your actions. So, if I am playing a violin, my brain will have an expectation of what sound it will make. If I play the expected note, my brain receives information that the outcome matched its prediction; if I hit an unexpected note, it receives information that it did not. In this experiment, we were able to measure these signals in real time while the instrument was being played,” said Joe Gibson, a Ph.D. researcher in the School of Physics and Astronomy. The recordings revealed changes in beta-wave activity following the lesson, providing evidence that even a short period of musical instruction can alter measurable patterns of brain function. The researchers also found a relationship between those neural changes and improvements in playing ability. Participants with the largest differences in beta-wave activity between the two scanning sessions also showed the greatest improvement in their violin performance. Although the findings do not establish that the changes in brain activity caused better playing, they suggest that beta oscillations are closely associated with how people acquire new motor skills. Making these measurements possible required expertise extending well beyond neuroscience. Professor Matthew Brookes of the University of Nottingham’s School of Physics and Astronomy has spent more than a decade leading the development of OPM-MEG technology. The violin experiment brought together specialists in physics, engineering, mathematics, and music to create a system capable of studying movement as it happens. “This is a study that we have been working on for years, and it’s taken a unique combination of skills: the physics required to measure brain activity; design engineering to create an ergonomic scanner that people can wear; the mathematics required to model the signals; and of course, Alan’s knowledge and abilities as a violin player and maker. Without this wonderful diversity of talent, we simply couldn’t have done the work.” The researchers believe the technology could eventually help scientists investigate more than musical learning. Some of the patterns of brain activity measured during the experiment can also be affected by neurological conditions, including dementia. Studying these signals during natural movements could offer another way to examine how brain function changes in health and disease. “The results provide a greater understanding of motor learning. It’s also fascinating that some of the effects that we measure here are among those that can be affected by disorders like dementia. Hopefully this type of study will bring about a new understanding of not just healthy brain function, but also disease,” said Brookes. Reference: “Beta-band dynamics during a naturalistic motor task: an OPM-MEG study” by Joseph Gibson, Jessikah Fildes, Alan Kirby, Niall Holmes, Lukas Rier, Karen J. Mullinger, Matias Ison, Peter G. Morris, Elena Boto, Ryan M. Hill and Matthew J. Brookes, 27 July 2026, bioRxiv . DOI: 10.64898/2026.07.27.740561 Disclosure: The University launched a spin-out company, Cerca Magnetics Limited, in 2020 to commercialize OPM-MEG scanners and related technologies. The wearable system has been installed in a number of high profile research institutions across the globe and is being used to investigate a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including epilepsy and dementia. Temporarily activating a protein best known for preventing cancer helped engineered human immune cells kill melanoma cells more effectively in the lab, suggesting a way to improve existing cell therapies. Engineering a patient’s immune cells to recognize cancer does not guarantee that they will keep fighting it. Repeated exposure to cancer can gradually weaken T cells’ ability to multiply and attack tumors, a decline known as exhaustion. The laboratory process used to prepare these cells for treatment can also make them mature too quickly, reducing their chances of surviving and remaining effective over time. These problems limit engineered T-cell therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy and T-cell receptor (TCR) therapy. Both involve collecting a patient’s immune cells, genetically modifying them in a laboratory to recognize cancer, and infusing them back into the patient to attack tumors. Such treatments have transformed care for certain blood cancers and are increasingly being investigated for solid tumors. Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a possible way to improve these cells during preparation. Their study, published in Frontiers in Immunology , found that temporarily activating a protein called p53 helped human T cells develop characteristics associated with longer-lasting immune responses and become more effective at killing melanoma cells in the laboratory. Often called the “guardian of the genome,” p53 is best known for preventing damaged cells from becoming cancerous. Scientists have extensively studied that protective role, but its involvement in regulating human T cells is less understood. The team collected human T cells and treated them with navtemadlin, an investigational drug that increases p53 activity by blocking another protein, MDM2. Normally, MDM2 keeps p53 levels under control. Comparing treated and untreated cells allowed the researchers to assess how activating p53 affected their development, energy production, and ability to fight cancer. To test cancer-killing performance, the researchers genetically engineered T cells to recognize a protein found on certain melanoma cells. They then used specialized imaging equipment to monitor the cells for nearly seven days. The engineered T cells prepared with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells than untreated cells. Their advantage became apparent after approximately 40 hours and continued throughout the experiment. They also showed improved cancer-fighting activity without additional interleukin-2, a protein commonly used to support T-cell growth and survival. “This is one of the first studies to link p53, one of the most extensively studied proteins in biology, to T-cell exhaustion in humans,” said Joseph Crompton, MD, PhD, assistant professor of surgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and senior author of the study. “While p53 has long been known for its role in preventing cancer, our findings suggest it may also play an important role in helping immune cells maintain their ability to fight it. This opens up a new avenue for developing more effective cancer immunotherapies.” The treated cells had greater energy reserves and were more likely to produce interferon-gamma and granzyme B, two cancer-fighting proteins that help immune cells coordinate an attack and destroy cancer cells. They were also more likely to develop into central memory T cells, which have a greater capacity to survive and multiply when they encounter their target again. Along with fewer molecular signs of exhaustion, this shift suggested that the cells might remain effective for longer. Those characteristics indicate potential for lasting immune responses, although the experiments tested human cells in the laboratory rather than treatment outcomes in patients. Adding a drug such as navtemadlin during cell preparation could potentially fit into existing manufacturing processes. That would offer a way to improve engineered T-cell therapies without developing an entirely new treatment or introducing additional genetic modifications. At lower concentrations, navtemadlin encouraged the development of healthy memory T cells without substantially reducing the overall number of viable cells. Higher concentrations, however, caused more cells to die, showing why any use of this approach would require careful control of p53 activation. Reference: “p53 activation via pharmacologic MDM2 inhibition constrains exhaustion and enhances antitumor function of human CD8+ T cells” by Alexandra Boix de Jesus, Hy B. Dao, Anthony Imani, Gabriel A. Rodriguez, Michael S. Shehata, Rachana R. Chandran, Stuart A. Fine, Sin Y. Lim, Michelle To, Serena Y. Lofftus, Nicolas Pedroncelli, Fritz C. Eilber, Brigitte N. Gomperts, Tyler R. McCaw, Cristina Puig-Saus and Joseph G. Crompton, 18 September 2026, Frontiers in Immunology . DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1910235 The study was funded in part by the American College of Surgeons, the UCLA Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research, the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, the Tower Cancer Research Foundation, the Sarcoma Foundation of America, and the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health under the Early-Stage Surgeon Scientist Program. Colorectal cancer rates in the United States are rising across a much wider range of ages than previously recognized, reversing a long period of declining diagnoses. A new study published in NEJM Evidence found that the increase is no longer concentrated among adults younger than 50, with rates now climbing in people approaching their 70s. Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths overall in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. As more generations reach ages when the disease becomes increasingly common, researchers warn that growing numbers of diagnoses could place additional demands on cancer treatment and long-term survivorship care. Researchers led by Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, analyzed National Cancer Institute data to track changes in colorectal cancer incidence over more than two decades. The age-adjusted rate dropped from 55.2 cases per 100,000 people in 2000 to 36.7 in 2022, before increasing to 38.3 in 2023. “This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years,” Murphy said. The study also found rising incidence across age groups through 65 to 69 years, indicating that the trend extends well beyond the younger populations that have received much of the attention. The increase among older adults is particularly concerning because colorectal cancer screening has historically produced substantial benefits in these age groups. Rates are now rising among people ages 65 to 69 and have stopped declining among those ages 70 to 74, despite approximately 80% of people in these groups being up to date with screening. Researchers suspect that unidentified risk factors may be counteracting some of the progress achieved through earlier detection and prevention. Murphy believes the expanding age range reflects a phenomenon known as the “birth cohort effect,” in which people born during particular periods experience different disease risks as they grow older. In this case, evidence suggests that individuals born in the 1960s and afterward may face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer that persists as they advance into middle and older adulthood. “I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time,” Murphy explained. “As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we’re going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.” The pattern could help connect the growing incidence among younger adults with the increases now appearing in older populations. American Cancer Society statistics show that colorectal cancer incidence among people ages 20 to 49 rose approximately 3% annually from 2013 to 2022. “There are many unique challenges when you’re diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it’s important that we shine a spotlight on that problem,” Murphy said. “But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.” The steepest increase occurred among adults ages 45 to 49, whose colorectal cancer incidence rose by 12.76% annually between 2019 and 2023. Researchers believe this unusually rapid increase largely reflects expanded screening following a change in national guidelines that lowered the recommended starting age from 50 to 45. Screening can temporarily raise reported incidence by detecting cancers that were already present but had not yet been diagnosed. “That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do — it’s catching cancer earlier,” Murphy said. However, increased screening cannot fully account for the broader rise across age groups, especially among older adults who already have high screening participation. The researchers also examined whether disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the trend. The increase persisted even when data from 2020 and 2021 were excluded, and screening activity had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels by January 2021. These findings suggest that pandemic-related delays are unlikely to explain the overall increase observed in 2023. The underlying causes of the rising incidence remain uncertain. Researchers are now examining whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could contribute to colorectal cancer risk, although no specific exposure has been established as responsible for the observed trends. “These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced,” said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine. Murphy is collaborating with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to investigate thousands of environmental chemical exposures using small blood samples. This approach will help identify substances that may warrant closer examination. The researchers then plan to work with Kupfer to study selected chemicals using colon organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce some features of human colon tissue. These models will allow scientists to investigate how particular exposures affect colon cells and potentially identify biological processes involved in cancer development. Until the causes become clearer, colorectal cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify the disease early and prevent deaths. Current national guidelines recommend routine screening for adults at average risk beginning at age 45 and continuing through age 75. Screening decisions outside that range should be individualized based on factors such as family history, symptoms, and other medical conditions. Colonoscopy remains the gold standard because it can both detect cancer and remove precancerous polyps. Other screening methods include home-based stool tests and newer blood-based tests, although their capabilities and recommended testing intervals differ. “There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated,” Kupfer added. For adults younger than 45 who do not qualify for routine screening, recognizing possible warning signs is particularly important. Blood in the stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, and unexplained weight loss should prompt medical evaluation, even in people without a known family history or genetic risk. The research team also recommends continued monitoring of national cancer registry data as new figures become available. If the upward trend persists as large generations of Americans grow older, healthcare systems may face increasing demand for cancer treatment, follow-up care, and long-term support for survivors.
